question: Evaluate $\int_0^1 \frac{(\tan^{-1}x)^2}{1+x^2}\,dx$ by making an appropriate substitution and changing the limits to the new variable before carrying out the integration.
explanation:
Consider

$$I=\int_0^1 \frac{(\tan^{-1}x)^2}{1+x^2}\,dx$$

The derivative of $\tan^{-1}x$ is $\frac{1}{1+x^2}$. Therefore, use the substitution

$$t=\tan^{-1}x$$

Then

$$dt=\frac{dx}{1+x^2}$$

The limits must be changed to the new variable. When $x=0$,

$$t=\tan^{-1}0=0$$

and when $x=1$,

$$t=\tan^{-1}1=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

Therefore, the given integral becomes

$$I=\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}t^2\,dt$$

Integrating,

$$I=\left[\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}}$$

$$I=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^3$$

$$I=\frac{\pi^3}{192}$$

Thus, after making the substitution and transforming the limits, the value of the definite integral is $\frac{\pi^3}{192}$.
